title: Sheriffs make plea for restraint, as House, Senate weigh more immigration enforcement limits
summary: Sheriffs traveled to Annapolis Wednesday with a message for lawmakers pushing a range of immigration protection proposals through the legislature: Don't place politics over public safety.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters February 26, 2026

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters February 26, 2026

Sheriffs traveled to Annapolis Wednesday with a message for lawmakers pushing a range of immigration protection proposals through the legislature: Don’t place politics over public safety.

The sheriffs’ visit came a week after Gov. Wes Moore (D) signed a bill into law that restricts agreements between local police and federal immigration officials,  and as both the House and Senate debate other measures aimed at providing new tools against policing abuses.

The House gave preliminary approval Wednesday to a combined bill that would allow prosecutors to use police surveillance techniques to “unmask” masked federal agents and to pursue court cases for civil rights violations. And the Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee listened to hours of testimony on bills limiting immigration activities by local police without a valid judicial warrant, and requiring local police to document” immigrant enforcement actions” by other agencies.

“They want to do everything they can to handcuff law enforcement, handcuff sheriffs across the state,” Frederick County Sheriff Chuck Jenkins said Wednesday.

Jenkins said sheriffs are continuing to consider a legal challenge to the new law to ban so-called 287(g) agreements. Frederick County was among nine counties to have agreements to detain any person undocumented in a jail for up to 48 hours for pickup by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement representative.

For about two hours Wednesday, the Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee discussed Senate Bill 791, the Community Trust Act, sponsored by Sen. Clarence Lam (D-Anne Arundel and Howard). The bill would prohibit local law enforcement agencies and jails from detaining any individuals based on immigration status unless there was a judicial warrant to do so. Local officials would not be allowed to act based on administrative warrants from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, the Justice Department “or any successor agency.”

Current law allows local law enforcement agencies to assist ICE through jail transfers and detain individuals without a warrant from a judge.

Lam said the bill would ensure “our jails would not be used as the front door to the federal government’s oftentimes deportation pipeline that we have seen over the last couple of months.”

Several senators questioned how the bill could restrict local authorities from ever working with federal authorities, specifically ICE.

Sen. Mary-Dulany James (D-Harford) expressed frustration with supporters who testified when she mentioned the family of Rachel Morin, who was raped and murdered by undocumented Salvadoran immigrant near her Harford County home in August 2023.

“When we rush, we’re impulsive. We throw things together that are experimental, untried [and] may have unintended consequences,” James said. “I’m sure the sponsor’s intentions are very good, as are yours, when we can actually be counterproductive in a way that’s very, very harmful.”

Alice Barrett, managing attorney for immigration services at We Are CASA, said the bill doesn’t restrict ICE from doing its job, such as issuing criminal warrants and conducting investigations.

House poised to approve bill creating tools to challenge federal agents in Maryland courts

Barrett acknowledged the deaths of Morin and others are tragic, but “they are not the vast majority of the individuals whom we are seeing.”

James immediately interjected.

“You would have to speak with her [Morin’s] mother about that and her children. I don’t think you would have the courage to say that straight to their family’s face,” she said.

An identical House version sponsored by Del. N. Scott Phillips (D-Baltimore County) was also discussed Wednesday before the Judiciary Committee.

According to the bills’ fiscal notes, “federal fund revenues may decrease significantly if the bill’s provisions are deemed as noncompliant with federal law.” That’s because of an executive order Trump signed on his first day in office, Jan. 20, 2025, that ordered the U.S. attorney general and the secretary of Homeland Security to “evaluate and undertake any lawful actions to ensure that so-called sanctuary jurisdictions, which seek to interfere with the lawful exercise of Federal law enforcement operations, do not receive access to Federal funds.”

Jenkins testified before the House committee, where Del. Gabriel Moreno (D-Howard County) asked if it was “your position that no undocumented immigrants should live in Maryland?”

“No one ever said that sir,” Jenkins said. “I’ve never mentioned anything about illegal immigrants. I’ve always been focused on criminals.”

The Senate committee also discussed Senate Bill 660 for nearly an hour. The bill is sponsored by Sen. Sara Love (D-Montgomery), who had her intern Eli Gendleman, a University of Maryland, Baltimore County senior summarize the bill.

It would require that whenever a local law enforcement agency is notified of immigration enforcement actions, an officer would have to go to the scene to observe and record what happened, then file a report to include the date, time and location, and if any medical attention was required. In addition, agencies would need to note if “officers were restricted from observing or recording the immigration enforcement action” and “preserve any evidence.”

“As we have seen time and time again, ICE putting out statements regarding its activities that are contradicted by local law enforcement or bystander video,” Gendleman said. “This legislation would ensure transparency and accountability.”

YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE.

Several sheriffs who testified disagree.

“This mandate places local agencies in a position of monitoring federal enforcement actions that are outside the scope of their authority, and certainly, their core mission as police officers,” said Wicomico County Sheriff Mike Lewis.

Some Democratic attorneys general spoke at a community event last month in Oregon, where they encouraged residents to use their cell phones to capture ICE activity, after the federal government tried to restrict access by state and local officials to evidence in the shooting death of Alex Pretti, 37, in Minneapolis.

“If you need to investigate something and ICE doesn’t turn it over, you can’t [investigate],” Love said Wednesday to the sheriffs who testified. “So if you have that evidence, then you can do your duties.”

Jenkins replied: “Is it our job to have oversight over ICE? I don’t believe it is. We simply don’t have the local manpower to do it.”
